title: Routing With the App Router
summary: Turn folders into URLs, wrap pages in layouts, read dynamic segments, navigate without reloads, and add loading, error, and 404 pages.
intro: A shop needs many pages: a home page, a list of products, a page for each product, help pages, an account page. In the React course you listed every route in code with React Router. In the App Router, the folders are the routes, and a handful of files with special names add the parts every app needs: a layout that stays on screen, a loading state, an error page, a 404. This lesson builds Trailhead's routes, shows how a URL is matched to a file, how pages read the parts of their URL, how links move between pages without a reload, and how the special files nest around each page.

steps.title: Folders become routes
steps.body:
Before you can add a page, you need to know where its file goes. In the App Router the answer is always the same: the folder path is the URL path, and a few naming rules let you organize files without changing a single URL.

```diagram routes-and-layouts-tree
Each page.tsx serves the URL its folders spell out. Folders in parentheses and folders starting with an underscore add nothing to the URL.
```

## A page makes a folder public

Each folder inside `app/` is a **route segment**, one piece of the URL between two slashes. `app/products/` is the segment `products`. A folder on its own serves nothing, though: only a `page.tsx` inside it makes the URL public. So `app/products/page.tsx` is the page at `/products`, and `app/page.tsx`, at the top, is the home page at `/`.

A page file's default export is a React component, and that component is the page. Name it anything you like. Next.js finds it by the file's name, not the function's.

## Colocation and private folders

Because only `page.tsx` makes something public, you can keep other files right next to the page that uses them: a component, a helper, a test. This is called **colocation**. A file like `app/products/product-grid.tsx` is never served at a URL of its own.

To say clearly that a folder is for code only, start its name with an underscore: `app/products/_components/` is a **private folder**, and Next.js skips it and everything inside it when it builds routes, even a `page.tsx`. Many teams keep shared code out of `app/` entirely, in folders like `components/` and `lib/` at the project's root, and colocate only what one route uses. Both work. Pick one and stick to it.

## Route groups

Sometimes you want to group routes without adding to the URL: say, the about, contact, and press pages share a narrow layout, and you want them in one folder. Wrap the folder's name in parentheses to make a **route group**: `app/(marketing)/about/page.tsx` is still the page at `/about`. The group can hold its own `layout.tsx`, which wraps only the pages inside it. Groups are also how you split a big app into areas, like `(shop)` and `(account)`, each with its own layout.

Two groups must not both claim the same URL. `app/(marketing)/about/page.tsx` and `app/(shop)/about/page.tsx` would both be `/about`, and the build stops with an error.

## Multiple root layouts

The root layout, `app/layout.tsx`, is the one that writes `html` and `body`. If two areas of your app need different documents altogether, say a marketing site and a dashboard with different fonts and themes, remove `app/layout.tsx` and give each top-level group its own root layout, each with its own `html` and `body`. The catch: moving between two root layouts loads a whole new page, not a soft navigation, since there's no shared layout to keep. Most apps need only one.

## Check the routes in the build

The route table that `npm run build` prints lists every URL the app serves, so it's the quickest way to check that your folders mean what you think. The example below is the table for Trailhead with the routes from the diagram.

examples.title: Trailhead's routes in the build

examples.explanation: Each line of the route table is a URL, not a folder. `/about` appears without `(marketing)`, since route groups are left out of the URL, and nothing from `_components` appears at all. `/products/[slug]` is one route with a **dynamic segment**, a piece of the URL that can be any value, which the part after next covers. The help pages show the same route listed four ways: once with its placeholder and once for each value the project listed ahead of time. The `○` and `◐` symbols say how each page is served, which the rendering lesson explains. For now, the table is a map of what a visitor can reach.

steps.title: Layouts and templates
steps.body:
Most pages share a frame: the site header, a footer, a side menu. If every page rendered its own copy, every click would rebuild the frame, flicker, and lose whatever state it held, like a half-typed search. Layouts solve that by staying put while the page inside them changes.

## The root layout

`app/layout.tsx` wraps every page in the app. It's the only file that writes `html` and `body`, and it's required: delete it, and Next.js asks for one. It's the right place for things every page shares, like the site header and the global CSS import.

## Nested layouts

Any folder can have its own `layout.tsx`, which wraps every page in that folder and below. Layouts nest: on `/products/ridge-2p-tent`, the root layout wraps `app/products/layout.tsx`, which wraps the product page. A layout receives the page, or the next layout down, as its `children` prop, and puts it wherever it likes.

The key behavior is what happens when you navigate:

```diagram routes-and-layouts-mounted
On a click from the list to a product, both layouts stay mounted, and only the page inside them is new.
```

Both pages live under `app/products/`, so both share the root layout and the products layout. When you click from the list to a product, React keeps those two layouts exactly as they are: same components, same state, no new render, no new request for them. Only the part that differs, the page, is fetched and swapped in. This is why the router can be so quick, and it's why a layout is the right home for anything that should survive navigation, like a search field or an open menu.

One consequence matters later, in the security lesson: since a layout doesn't render again when you move between its pages, it's the wrong place for the only check that a user may see a page. Each page has to check for itself.

## Pages you leave are kept, hidden

Next.js goes one step further with Cache Components on. A page you navigate away from isn't thrown away: it's hidden with React's `Activity` component, which you met in the React course, and kept, up to three pages. Press Back, and the page comes back exactly as you left it, scroll position, open sections, and typed text included. Usually that's what you want. When it isn't, say a dropdown that should be closed when you return, the component has to reset that state itself.

## Templates remount

A `template.tsx` file looks like a layout, a component that receives `children`, but it does the opposite on navigation: it's given a new React key each time its segment changes, so it and every client component inside it are created fresh. Its effects run again too. Use a template when something should restart on every page in a folder, like an entrance animation, or a feedback form that should be empty for each product. It sits inside the layout of the same folder, so the layout still stays.

## Typed props with LayoutProps

Next.js generates types for your routes as you run `next dev` or `next build`. `LayoutProps<"/products">` is the props a layout at `/products` gets: `children`, plus a prop for each named slot, which the last part of this lesson covers. `PageProps` does the same for pages. They're global, so you use them without an import, and a typo in the route's name is a type error.

examples.title: A layout for every products page
examples.prompt: `app/products/layout.tsx` puts the category links above every page under `/products`.
examples.explanation: `children` is the matched page: the list at `/products`, or a product at `/products/ridge-2p-tent`. The layout itself is rendered once when you first arrive under `/products` and then kept, so the category links don't flicker as you move between products. `CategoryNav` lives in the private `_components` folder next to the layout, since nothing else uses it. It's a client component that reads the URL's search string to mark the current category, which is why it sits inside `Suspense`: the part on navigating explains that rule. The empty `div` with a fixed height holds its place until it's ready, so the page below doesn't jump.

examples.title: A template that starts fresh
examples.prompt: `app/products/[slug]/template.tsx` wraps each product page in a fade-in that plays again on every product you open.
examples.explanation: A template takes `children` like a layout, but Next.js gives it a new key whenever its own segment, here the product's slug, changes. So moving from one product to another throws this `div` away and creates a new one, and a CSS entrance animation on it plays again. If it were a layout, the `div` would stay, and the animation would play only once. Search params don't count as a change: going from `?color=red` to `?color=blue` on the same product keeps the template. Reach for a template only when you need this. Most folders need only a layout.

steps.title: Dynamic segments
steps.body:
A shop with twelve products shouldn't need twelve page files, and a shop with twelve thousand certainly can't have them. A **dynamic segment** is one folder that matches any value in its place in the URL, and the page reads the value to decide what to show.

## Square brackets

Wrap a folder's name in square brackets, and it matches any single segment: `app/products/[slug]/page.tsx` serves `/products/ridge-2p-tent`, `/products/ember-stove`, and every other product. The name inside the brackets, `slug`, is the key the value arrives under. A **slug** is the short, readable name of a thing in a URL.

Two more forms catch more than one segment:

- `[...topic]` is a **catch-all**: it matches one or more segments. `app/help/[...topic]` serves `/help/shipping` and `/help/shipping/fees`, and the page gets `["shipping", "fees"]`. It does not match `/help` alone.
- `[[...topic]]`, in double brackets, is an **optional catch-all**: the same, plus `/help` itself, where the value is missing.

## params is a promise

The page receives the values as a prop called `params`, and in Next.js 16 it's a promise, so you `await` it. Search parameters, the `?category=tents` part of a URL, arrive the same way in a prop called `searchParams`, also a promise. Both are promises so that Next.js can start rendering everything that doesn't need them before the values are known. The data lessons show how that lets most of a page be ready ahead of time.

`PageProps<"/products/[slug]">` types both props for that route: `params` resolves to `{ slug: string }`, a catch-all gives `string[]`, and an optional catch-all gives `string[] | undefined`.

## The Trailhead API

From here on, the product pages get their data from the Trailhead API, so it has to be running while you try the shop. To run it, [add the Trailhead API to your Playground](/playground?add=trailhead-api). The link puts a `trailhead-api` folder at the Playground's top level, next to `trailhead`, with `server.mjs`, `openapi.yaml`, the product photos in `images/`, and a README, and it never writes over files that are already there. The API names each photo by a path like `/images/products/trail-pack-45.webp`, which the app serves from its `public` folder, so copy the photos in once, from the Playground folder:

```bash
cp -r trailhead-api/images trailhead/public/
```

Then start the API in a second terminal, from the Playground folder:

```bash
node trailhead-api/server.mjs
```

It prints `Trailhead API on http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1` and keeps running until you press Ctrl+C. Point the shop at it with the line `API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1` in `trailhead/.env`. The data and rendering lessons start it as `TRAILHEAD_DELAYS=1 node trailhead-api/server.mjs`, which slows its answers down like a real network, so loading states and streaming are easy to see.

## When the value isn't real

Anyone can type `/products/nope`. When the page finds no product for the slug, it calls `notFound()` from `next/navigation`. That stops rendering the page right there and shows the nearest `not-found.tsx` instead. `notFound()` works by throwing a special error, so nothing after it runs, and TypeScript knows that: after `if (!product) notFound();`, it treats `product` as defined.

## Values Next.js can't know ahead of time

With Cache Components on, Next.js renders as much of every page as it can during the build, before anyone visits. A slug that's only known when someone opens the URL can't be part of that early render, so the page needs something to show in its place while it's worked out. The simplest answer is a `loading.tsx` file next to the page, which shows its content while the page waits. Without one, the build stops and says the route accessed `params` outside of `Suspense`. The other answer is to list the values ahead of time with `generateStaticParams`, a function the page exports that returns them. The help pages do that in the example below, and the rendering lesson covers it in depth.

examples.title: One page for every product
examples.prompt: `app/products/[slug]/page.tsx`. `getProduct` is a function in `lib/products.ts` that calls the Trailhead API and returns `null` for an unknown slug. The data lessons write it.
examples.explanation:
The page is `async`, so it can wait for `params` and then for the product. For `/products/ridge-2p-tent`, `slug` is `"ridge-2p-tent"`. An unknown slug makes `getProduct` return `null`, and `notFound()` shows the not-found page instead of a crash. Next to this file sits `app/products/[slug]/loading.tsx`, a component that returns `

Loading product…

`. It shows while the page waits for its slug and its data, and it's also what lets the build succeed, since the slug isn't known until someone opens the URL. `formatPrice` turns integer cents into text like $349.00.

examples.title: Help pages with an optional catch-all
examples.prompt: `app/help/[[...topic]]/page.tsx` serves `/help` and every path under it, and lists three of them ahead of time.
examples.explanation: At `/help`, `topic` is `undefined`, and the heading says Help: all topics. At `/help/shipping/fees` it's `["shipping", "fees"]`, and the heading says Help: shipping / fees. `generateStaticParams` returns the values Next.js should render during the build: an empty list for `/help` itself, then `shipping` and `returns`. Those three come out as complete static pages, the `○` lines in the route table you saw earlier. Any other topic still works: the first visitor gets it rendered on the spot, and Next.js keeps the result for the next one.

steps.title: Navigating between pages
steps.body:
A plain link loads a whole new document, throws away every bit of state on the page, and downloads the shared parts again. In a Next.js app that's slow and wasteful, because the router can fetch just the part of the page that changes. To get that, you navigate with the router's tools, not with plain `a` tags or `window.location`.

## Link

`Link` from `next/link` renders an ordinary `a` tag with a real `href`, so it works before JavaScript loads, can be opened in a new tab, and is read correctly by screen readers and search engines. Once the page has hydrated, a click on it becomes a soft navigation: the router fetches the new page's RSC payload and swaps in only what changed, as the previous lesson showed. Back and Forward work the same way, through the History API you met in the web course.

In a production build, `Link` also **prefetches**. When a link scrolls into view, the router quietly downloads the **App Shell** of the page it points to: the parts of that page that are the same for every visitor and every URL, like its layouts and loading states. With Partial Prefetching on, as it is in a new project, one shell per route is shared by every link to it, so a list of twelve product links fetches the product page's shell once. A click then shows that shell at once while the rest arrives. You can turn prefetching off for a link with `prefetch={false}`, or ask for the whole page ahead of time, not just its shell, with `prefetch={true}`.

## Hooks for client components

Three hooks from `next/navigation` work in client components, the ones that run in the browser:

- `usePathname()` returns the current path, like `/products/ridge-2p-tent`. Use it to mark the current link in a menu.
- `useSearchParams()` returns the search parameters, read-only, with `.get("category")`.
- `useRouter()` returns the router, for navigating from code: `router.push("/cart")` after an action, `router.back()`, or `router.refresh()` to fetch the current page again from the server.

These read **URL data**, the parts of the URL that differ from link to link. Next.js prerenders one shell for a route like `/products/[slug]` before it knows which product you'll open, so a component that reads URL data can't be part of it. With Cache Components on, such a component must sit inside a `Suspense` boundary, and its fallback stands in for it until the URL is known. Forget the boundary, and the build names the hook and the file. That's why the category links and the menu links in the examples sit inside `Suspense`.

## Redirects

To send a visitor somewhere else from a Server Component, call `redirect("/login")` from `next/navigation`. Like `notFound()`, it throws, so nothing after it runs. It answers with a `307 Temporary Redirect` on a page load, the right code for a redirect that depends on the moment, like a login check. `permanentRedirect("/products")` answers `308 Permanent Redirect` instead, for an address that moved for good, so search engines update their links. Like `notFound()`, a redirect that happens after the page has started streaming can't change the status anymore, so Next.js sends a tag that makes the browser follow it instead. Both also work inside Server Actions, the form handlers you'll meet in a later lesson. For many old addresses at once, the `redirects` option in `next.config.ts` handles them before any page runs.

## State survives navigation

Since layouts stay mounted, any state in them survives a click, just as a layout route's state survived in React Router. And since pages you leave are kept hidden for a while, Back brings them back with their state too. Changing only the search parameters, like `?category=packs` to `?category=tents`, renders the same page again with new values, and the page's client components keep their state.

examples.title: A menu link that knows where you are
examples.prompt: `components/nav-link.tsx` is a client component, so it can read the current path.
examples.explanation: `"use client"` at the top makes this a client component, which the next lesson explains in full. It's needed because `usePathname` is a hook, and hooks only run in client components. The link counts as current on its own page and on any page below it, so Products stays marked on a product page. `aria-current="page"` tells screen readers which link is the current page, and a CSS rule like `[aria-current="page"] { text-decoration: underline; }` can style it, so one attribute serves both. Setting it to `undefined` leaves the attribute off entirely on other links.

examples.title: The header that uses it
examples.prompt: `components/site-header.tsx`, rendered by the root layout. Each menu link sits inside its own `Suspense` boundary.
examples.explanation: The header is a Server Component, and it's on every page, `/products/[slug]` included, where the path isn't known when the shell is made. Each `NavLink` reads the path, so each one sits inside `Suspense` with a fallback: a plain `Link` with the same label and address. The fallback goes into the shell, so the menu shows and works at once, and the marked version replaces it a moment later. Without the boundaries, the build fails with an error that names `usePathname()` and this file. The fallback looks almost the same as the real link, so nothing jumps.

examples.title: A permanent redirect
examples.prompt: `app/catalog/page.tsx` sends the shop's old address to the new one, with `permanentRedirect("/products")` as its only line. Ask for the old address with the production server running.
examples.explanation: `-I` asks for the status line and headers only, and `head -1` keeps the first line. `308 Permanent Redirect` tells browsers and search engines that the page has moved for good. The `location: /products` header further down says where to. 308 is the modern version of 301 that also keeps the request's method, so a POST stays a POST. A browser follows it at once, and a search engine updates its link. Since nothing about this page depends on who asks, Next.js renders the redirect during the build, like any static page.

steps.title: Loading, error, and not-found files
steps.body:
Every real app has pages that are slow, that fail, or that don't exist. Next.js gives each of those a file with a special name, so the right thing appears in the right place without any code to wire it up. You only need to know where each file applies.

```diagram routes-and-layouts-boundaries
In each folder, Next.js nests the special files from the outside in. A file catches what happens inside its box.
```

## loading.tsx

A `loading.tsx` file shows while its folder's page, and anything below it, is still rendering. Under the hood, Next.js wraps the page in a React `Suspense` boundary, recalled from the React course, with your loading component as the fallback. The layout above it shows at once, so the header and menus appear immediately and only the page area waits. It's also part of the shell that `Link` prefetches, so a click shows it straight away.

A loading file covers the whole page. When only one part of a page is slow, like reviews under a product, put a `Suspense` boundary around just that part instead, and the rest of the page can show sooner. The lesson on data fetching shows how to choose.

## error.tsx

An `error.tsx` file catches errors thrown while rendering anything below it, a failed fetch for example, and shows itself in their place. The layouts above it keep working, so a visitor can still use the menus and move on. It must be a client component, since it's built on a React error boundary, and it gets two props:

- `error`, what was thrown. In production, an error from a Server Component reaches the browser with a generic message and a `digest`, a short code that matches the full error in the server's log. That keeps details like database messages from leaking to visitors.
- `retry`, a function that tries again: it fetches and renders the failed part once more, which often works when the problem was a brief network blip.

An `error.tsx` doesn't catch errors in the layout of its own folder, since it sits inside that layout. To catch those, put one in the folder above. For the root layout itself there's `app/global-error.tsx`, which replaces the whole document when it shows, so it writes its own `html` and `body`.

## not-found.tsx

A `not-found.tsx` file is what `notFound()` shows. The nearest one above the page that called it wins, so `app/products/[slug]/not-found.tsx` can say we don't sell that, while `app/not-found.tsx` handles every address that matches no route at all.

One detail surprises people. Once a page starts streaming, the status line has already gone out as `200`, so a `notFound()` called while the product loads can't change it to `404`. Next.js adds a `meta` tag telling search engines not to index the page instead. When the status code itself must be `404` from the first visit, check the slug before streaming starts, in proxy, which a later lesson covers. The rendering lesson shows how listing slugs ahead of time gets you a real `404` from the second visit on.

## How they nest

Inside one folder the order is fixed: the layout, then the template, then the error boundary, then the loading boundary, then the not-found boundary, then the page. When the URL goes deeper, the next folder's layout takes the page's place, with its own set of files inside. So each file covers everything below it, and the closest one wins. An error in a product page is caught by `app/products/[slug]/error.tsx` if there is one, and otherwise by `app/products/error.tsx`, which still leaves the root layout's header working.

examples.title: An error page for the products section
examples.explanation: `error` is typed `unknown`, since anything can be thrown, so the code checks that it's an `Error` with a `digest` before reading it. Showing the digest gives a visitor a code to quote when they report the problem, and you can search the server's log for it. With the Trailhead API stopped, the products page showed this box with the code 2771098206, and the terminal running `npm run start` printed `TypeError: fetch failed` with the same digest and the real cause, `ECONNREFUSED`. `role="alert"` makes screen readers announce the message. The category links above it, from the products layout, kept working.

examples.title: A streamed 404
examples.prompt: With the production server running, ask for a product that doesn't exist, and pick out the status line and the robots tag.
examples.explanation: The status is `200 OK`, although the page shows the product not-found page. The shell, with the header and the Loading product… fallback, was already on its way with a 200 when the page learned the slug was unknown. So Next.js added the `noindex` tag, which tells search engines to leave the page out of their results, and swapped in the not-found page. A browser user sees the right page either way. If a real `404` status matters, for an analytics tool or a strict crawler, handle unknown slugs before streaming starts, in proxy, which a later lesson covers. `/no-such-page`, which matches no route at all, does answer `404 Not Found`.

steps.title: Parallel and intercepting routes
steps.body:
Some screens show two pages at once. The classic case is a quick view: you click a product in the list, its details open in a dialog over the list, and the URL changes to the product's own address, so you can share it or reload it. Two special folder conventions build that, and they're worth recognizing even if you use them rarely.

## Slots

A folder whose name starts with `@` is a **slot**, a named place in a layout for a second page. `app/products/@modal/` is a slot called `modal`, and the products layout receives it as a prop next to `children`, rendering both. A slot isn't a route segment, so it adds nothing to the URL: for each URL, Next.js picks a page for `children` and a page for each slot. These are **parallel routes**, since several pages render side by side.

When a slot has no page for the current URL, Next.js needs to know what to put there, and that's what `default.tsx` in the slot is for. It renders on a full page load when nothing in the slot matches. For a modal, it returns `null`: no dialog. In Next.js 16 it's required, and the build stops with an error that names the layout and the missing file when a slot lacks one.

## Intercepting routes

The second piece decides when the dialog appears. A folder named `(.)[slug]` inside the slot **intercepts** the route `[slug]` at the same level. When a soft navigation, a click on a `Link`, goes to `/products/ridge-2p-tent` from inside `/products`, the router renders the intercepting page into the `modal` slot, and the list stays in `children` underneath. A direct visit or a reload of the same URL isn't intercepted: it shows the real product page. Other prefixes reach further: `(..)` intercepts a segment one level up, and `(...)` one from the root of `app`.

## The modal pattern

Put together, a click opens the dialog with the product's URL in the address bar. Back closes it, Forward opens it again, a shared link opens the full product page, and a reload does too. That's hard to get right by hand, and here it's all folders.

It's also more moving parts than most features need. Skip it when the content doesn't need its own URL, like a confirmation or a small form, and use a plain dialog in a client component instead. And remember that the page you leave is hidden, not removed, as the part on layouts explained, so a closed dialog's component may still be in the document, out of sight, until it's evicted.

## What the files look like

The examples below are the three files Trailhead uses: the layout with the slot, the empty default, and the intercepting page. The dialog component itself, `components/modal.tsx`, is a small client component that renders a `dialog` element and calls `router.back()` when it closes. Leave out `app/products/@modal/default.tsx`, and the build stops with three errors, among them `Parallel route slots cannot render the same URLs`, naming `app/products/layout.tsx` and the URLs that need a default.

examples.title: The layout with a modal slot
examples.prompt: `app/products/layout.tsx`, now taking the `modal` slot as a prop next to `children`.
examples.explanation: Next.js passes one prop per slot, named after the folder without the `@`, so `@modal` arrives as `modal`. `LayoutProps<"/products">` knows about it, since the types are generated from the folders, and leaving it out of the props is a type error. Rendering `{modal}` after `{children}` puts the dialog after the list in the document. Most of the time the slot holds `default.tsx`, which renders nothing, so the layout looks just as it did before.

examples.title: The slot's default
examples.prompt: `app/products/@modal/default.tsx`, what the slot shows when no page in it matches.
examples.explanation: Returning `null` means no dialog. Next.js uses this file on a full page load, or a reload, of any URL under `/products` that the slot has no page for, which is every URL here except an intercepted product. Without it, the slot has nothing it may render for `/products` and `/products/[slug]`, so the build refuses to continue.

examples.title: The intercepting page
examples.prompt: `app/products/@modal/(.)[slug]/page.tsx` renders a product into the dialog when a link inside `/products` opens it.
examples.explanation: The page doesn't await `params` itself. It hands the promise to `QuickViewBody` inside `Suspense`, so the dialog appears at once with Loading… and fills in when the product arrives. `Pick<..., "params">` reuses the page's types for the child's one prop. Clicking Ridge 2P Tent in the list opened a dialog reading Ridge 2P Tent, $349.00, with the list still underneath and the address bar at `/products/ridge-2p-tent`. Reloading the same address showed the full product page from `app/products/[slug]/page.tsx` instead, with no dialog. Several files in this lesson started with `"use client"`. The next lesson explains what that line does, and how to choose where each component runs.

recap:
- A folder in app/ is a URL segment, and only a page.tsx inside it makes the URL public.
- Folders in parentheses group routes without changing URLs, and folders starting with an underscore are private.
- Layouts wrap their folder's pages and stay mounted on navigation. Templates remount, and pages you leave are kept hidden for Back.
- [slug], [...slug], and [[...slug]] match one, many, or optionally many segments, read from the params promise.
- Link navigates softly and prefetches each route's App Shell. Hooks that read the URL need a Suspense boundary.
- loading.tsx, error.tsx, and not-found.tsx nest in a fixed order, and the nearest one above a page wins.
- A streamed page has already sent a 200, so notFound() then adds a noindex tag instead of a 404.
- @slot folders render pages side by side, need a default.tsx, and (.) folders intercept a route for modals.
